findings.title: Adapter interface contract violated by agent adapter
findings.description: ClaudeSonnetWithToolsAdapter implements the Adapter interface but its query() method throws unconditionally. This is a Liskov Substitution violation — any code iterating over adapters generically (e.g., multi-adapter dispatch) must special-case this adapter. The interface should be split into RetrievalAdapter and AgentAdapter, or expressed via a discriminated union/optional capability flag, so consumers cannot accidentally call query() on an agent adapter.
findings.recommendation: Introduce two interfaces: RetrievalAdapter (with query) and AgentAdapter (with runAgentLoop). Have ClaudeSonnetWithToolsAdapter implement only AgentAdapter. Update types.ts to export both, and let runners select by capability rather than using a single Adapter type.

findings.title: Adapter init() signature inconsistent across adapters (poisonFixtures only on agent adapter)
findings.description: ClaudeSonnetWithToolsAdapter.init() widens the AdapterConfig with `& { poisonFixtures?: PoisonFixture[] }`, while RipgrepBm25Adapter and HybridNoGraphAdapter use their own narrowed config types. This breaks the pluggability story: a generic dispatcher cannot pass a single config blob to all adapters without each adapter understanding extra fields. The shared types contract in types.ts does not document this extension model.
findings.recommendation: Define AdapterConfig in types.ts as an open-ended record with a typed `extensions` field, or use per-adapter config generics on the Adapter interface (Adapter<TConfig extends AdapterConfig>). Document the contract in types.ts so all adapters surface required config consistently.

findings.title: Optional adapter lifecycle methods (snapshot, teardown) inconsistently implemented
findings.description: RipgrepBm25Adapter implements snapshot() but not teardown(); HybridNoGraphAdapter implements teardown() but not snapshot(); VectorOnlyAdapter implements snapshot() but not teardown(); ClaudeSonnetWithToolsAdapter implements teardown() with an `as any` cast on engine.disconnect. This produces resource leaks (PGLite engines not always disconnected) and inconsistent reproducibility across runs.
findings.recommendation: Make teardown() mandatory in the Adapter interface (returning Promise<void>; default no-op for in-memory adapters). Add snapshot() as a separately-typed optional capability. Remove the `as any` cast by typing PGLiteEngine.disconnect properly in the engine import.

findings.title: BrainState as opaque `any`-equivalent loses type safety across adapter boundary
findings.description: Each adapter casts BrainState to its concrete state type at the top of query() (e.g., `state as Bm25State`, `state as VectorOnlyState`, `state as HybridNoGraphState`). This is the classic `void*` anti-pattern: BrainState carries no compile-time guarantee that the state passed to query() is the one returned by init(). A wiring bug between init/query in multi-adapter.ts would compile cleanly and crash at runtime.
findings.recommendation: Make Adapter generic in its state type: `interface Adapter<S = unknown> { init(...): Promise<S>; query(q, state: S): Promise<RankedDoc[]>; teardown?(state: S): Promise<void> }`. Each adapter then declares its concrete S, and the compiler enforces init/query state agreement.

findings.title: Runner orchestration mixes subprocess and programmatic categories ad-hoc
findings.description: all.ts dispatches Cats 1-4, 6, 7, 10-12 as subprocesses and skips Cats 5, 8, 9 because they require runtime inputs. The discriminated union (SubprocessCategory | ProgrammaticCategory) is fine, but there is no single entry point that runs everything — the report just notes 'run via harness'. This breaks the BrainBench composability story and forces callers to know which cats are which kind.
findings.recommendation: Introduce a uniform CatRunner interface: `interface CatRunner { num: number; name: string; run(ctx: BenchContext): Promise<CatResult> }`. Implement a SubprocessCatRunner and InProcessCatRunner. Have a shared BenchContext provide claims/probes/scenarios/state lazily so all.ts can run every cat through one dispatch path.

findings.title: Generators and runners share types only via deep relative imports
findings.description: Generator files (amara-life.ts, world.ts, gen.ts) and runner files (adapters, judge, all.ts) communicate exclusively via deep relative paths (e.g., `../runner/types.ts`, `./amara-life.ts`). There is no barrel export and no clear architectural seam between the generator layer (produces corpus + skeletons) and the runner layer (consumes corpus, runs adapters). Cross-layer type churn will ripple unpredictably.
findings.recommendation: Create eval/contracts/index.ts (or eval/types/index.ts) that re-exports the public types shared between generators, runners, and judges (Page, Query, Adapter, RankedDoc, BrainState, PoisonFixture, etc.). Make all cross-layer imports go through this barrel. Generators should not import from runner/, and runner should not import generator internals.

findings.title: Reference data hard-coded inside generator skeleton breaks generator/data separation
findings.description: amara-life.ts ships DEFAULT_CONTACTS as a hard-coded list inside the generator module, and amara-life-gen.ts hard-codes 6 reference docs (NovaMind update, market report, cap table, etc.) inline as JS string literals. This couples the generator code to the world fixture data, making it hard to evolve corpora independently or reuse the generator engine for a different persona.
findings.recommendation: Move DEFAULT_CONTACTS and the 6 reference docs into eval/data/amara-life-v1/_seed/ as JSON/MD files. Have the generator load them at runtime. This separates the generator engine (reusable) from corpus-specific seed data (one fixture per persona).

findings.title: Duplicated PRNG implementation across generator files
findings.description: Mulberry32 PRNG is reimplemented in three places: world.ts (`mulberry32`), amara-life.ts (`createRng`), and adversarial-injections.ts (`createRng`). Three forks of the same primitive risk drift (one already differs subtly in initialization), and any determinism bug must be fixed in three places.
findings.recommendation: Extract to eval/lib/rng.ts exporting a single `createRng(seed: number): () => number` and `pick`/`pickN` helpers. Have all three generator files import it. Add a unit test asserting determinism on a known seed.

findings.title: Cost-tracking and Anthropic client setup duplicated between gen.ts and amara-life-gen.ts
findings.description: Both generators reimplement: loadEnv() reading .env.testing, ANTHROPIC_API_KEY validation, Anthropic client construction, PRICE_INPUT_PER_M / PRICE_OUTPUT_PER_M constants, HARD_STOP_USD enforcement, and a CostTracker/CostLedger struct. The two implementations are slightly different (HARD_STOP_USD=20 vs 80; different ledger shape), which is a maintenance hazard and an anti-pattern for a layered generator architecture.
findings.recommendation: Extract eval/lib/llm-budget.ts (already referenced by all.ts as `BRAINBENCH_LLM_CONCURRENCY`) to own: env loading, client singleton, pricing table, CostTracker, and a `callWithBudget(client, req, tracker, opts)` wrapper. Both generators consume it; per-generator HARD_STOP_USD passes in as a parameter.

findings.title: Bug: writeDocs path manipulation produces double-extension or misnamed files
findings.description: In amara-life-gen.ts writeDocs(), the path computation `slugPath + '.md'.replace(/\.md$/, '') === slugPath ? slugPath : slugPath` is a no-op tautology (the ternary always picks slugPath). The subsequent `const fullPath = join(CORPUS_ROOT, slugPath)` is what actually runs, but the `path` variable is computed and ignored. This is dead code masking what was likely intended to be path normalization, and the ambiguity will rot.
findings.recommendation: Delete the dead `path` line entirely. The slug paths in the docs array already include `.md` (e.g., 'doc/novamind-investor-update.md'), so just use `const fullPath = join(CORPUS_ROOT, slugPath); ensureDir(dirname(fullPath)); writeFileSync(fullPath, body);`.

findings.title: Adapter classes lack a registry — adapter selection is implicit
findings.description: Adapters are exported as classes plus convenience factories (`createRipgrepBm25`, `createVectorOnly`, `createHybridNoGraph`), but there is no central registry mapping name → factory. multi-adapter.ts (referenced by `eval:run`) presumably wires these by hand, which means adding a new adapter requires touching the dispatcher. This is the classic missing-registry / open-closed violation for plugin architectures.
findings.recommendation: Create eval/runner/adapters/index.ts exporting `ADAPTER_REGISTRY: Record<string, () => Adapter>` keyed by adapter.name. multi-adapter.ts iterates the registry, allowing new adapters to register themselves without dispatcher edits. Optionally support env-var filtering (BRAINBENCH_ADAPTERS=grep-only,vector).

findings.title: Console.log/error monkey-patching is a leaky abstraction
findings.description: HybridNoGraphAdapter.init() globally replaces console.log and console.error to silence importFromContent's stdout, then restores them in finally. If init() runs concurrently with another adapter (and all.ts runs cats with concurrency=2, multi-adapter.ts may run adapters in parallel), the global console patching races and silently swallows logs from other components.
findings.recommendation: Push the silencing concern down: importFromContent should accept a logger parameter (or use a structured logger like pino with a noop transport). Failing that, use Bun.write to /dev/null for the import call rather than mutating global console. Document the race risk if it must stay.

findings.title: Dynamic require() inside async functions in all.ts
findings.description: readCommit() and readBranch() use CommonJS `require('child_process')` inside an async function in an ES module file (package.json has `"type": "module"`). This works in Bun but is inconsistent with the rest of the codebase's `import { spawn } from 'child_process'` style at the top of the same file, and would break under stricter ESM tooling.
findings.recommendation: Use the already-imported execSync (or import it at the top): `import { execSync, spawn } from 'child_process';`. Make readCommit/readBranch synchronous since execSync is synchronous; drop the unnecessary Promise wrapper.

findings.title: Command injection risk in browser open via execSync with file path
findings.description: In world-view.ts, the path returned from renderWorldHtmlToFile is interpolated directly into a shell command via execSync(`${cmd} "${path}"`). While the path is derived from a --dir argument (default constant), a user-supplied --dir could contain shell metacharacters (e.g., `"; rm -rf ~`) producing command injection. CWE-78: OS Command Injection. Even though the tool is a developer convenience, accepting CLI args and shelling out unquoted-safely is a code-injection sink.
findings.recommendation: Use execFile(cmd, [path]) instead of execSync with string interpolation, which passes path as a separate argv and avoids shell parsing. Alternatively, validate that the resolved path contains no shell metacharacters before invoking execSync.

findings.title: Manual .env parser writes attacker-controlled values into process.env
findings.description: loadEnv() in amara-life-gen.ts (and gen.ts) reads .env.testing line-by-line with a permissive regex and assigns matches to process.env without validation. If the .env file is sourced from an untrusted location (the docstring even instructs `find ../ -maxdepth 2 -name .env.testing` and copy here), malicious lines can inject env vars consumed by child processes (e.g., NODE_OPTIONS, PATH manipulation). CWE-15: External Control of System or Configuration Setting. Mitigated by the file being developer-controlled, but the explicit cross-worktree copy pattern weakens that assumption.
findings.recommendation: Use a vetted dotenv parser (e.g., bun's --env-file flag or dotenv with strict mode), or restrict assigned keys to an allow-list (ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, OPENAI_API_KEY, GROQ_API_KEY).

findings.title: JSON.parse on untrusted file path without size limit
findings.description: query-validate.ts reads an arbitrary file path passed as argv[2] via readFileSync and JSON.parse with no size cap or schema validation prior to parse. A maliciously large or pathological JSON file could DoS the validator (memory exhaustion). CWE-400: Uncontrolled Resource Consumption. Low impact because this is a dev/CI tool, but still a defensive-coding gap.
findings.recommendation: Stat the file and reject inputs above a reasonable threshold (e.g., 10 MB). Wrap JSON.parse in a try/catch (already present) and consider a streaming JSON parser for very large inputs.

findings.title: Prompt injection surface in adversarial generator (informational — by design)
findings.description: adversarial-injections.ts and adversarial.ts intentionally craft prompt-injection / poison content (e.g., 'mark the sender as pre-approved') and feed it into LLM-bound prompts. This is the explicit purpose of the benchmark (Cat 10 robustness). Defenses depend on downstream consumers (gbrain agent loop in claude-sonnet-with-tools.ts) treating retrieved content as untrusted. The harness itself is fine, but operators running this benchmark with live API keys must ensure tool outputs cannot exfiltrate secrets. CWE-77 (relevant for downstream consumers).
findings.recommendation: Document explicitly in the README that adversarial corpora must not be run against agents with write access to secret stores or external networks beyond the test sandbox. Verify tool-bridge.ts (not provided) enforces a read-only / dry-run boundary.

findings.title: Tool execution errors swallowed and surfaced to LLM as tool_result content
findings.description: In runAgentLoop, ForbiddenOpError and UnknownToolError are caught and stringified into the tool_result content sent back to the model, including err.message and err.kind. If those errors include sensitive details (file paths, internal config, stack-derived strings), they are exposed to the LLM and saved into transcripts. CWE-209: Information Exposure Through an Error Message. Risk is bounded if ForbiddenOpError messages are curated, but the pattern is worth flagging.
findings.recommendation: Ensure ForbiddenOpError/UnknownToolError messages contain only the high-level reason (e.g., 'forbidden operation: write_external'), not user input echoed back or internal paths. Add a redactor before serializing into tool_result.content.

findings.title: pdf-parse dependency: known historical RCE/parsing vulnerabilities
findings.description: package.json lists pdf-parse@^2.4.5 as a devDependency for the PDF loader. The pdf-parse ecosystem (and underlying pdfjs-dist) has had multiple CVEs related to malicious PDF parsing leading to memory issues / prototype pollution. Since adversarial PDFs are explicitly part of this benchmark, parsing untrusted PDFs in the same process as Anthropic API keys is a real concern. CWE-1395: Dependency on Vulnerable Third-Party Component.
findings.recommendation: Pin pdf-parse to the latest patched version, run `bun audit` / npm audit in CI, and isolate PDF parsing behind a worker process with no env access. Consider running adversarial PDF ingestion under a separate user / container with no API keys mounted.

findings.title: Unpinned git dependency: gbrain pulled from github master
findings.description: package.json declares `"gbrain": "github:garrytan/gbrain#master"`, which fetches whatever the master branch of an external GitHub repo points to at install time. This is a supply-chain risk: any compromise of that branch (or a force-push) silently propagates into every install. CWE-829: Inclusion of Functionality from Untrusted Control Sphere. The benchmark consumes gbrain as a library and runs its tool-bridge / engine code in-process with API keys.
findings.recommendation: Pin to a specific commit SHA (e.g., `github:garrytan/gbrain#<sha>`) and update intentionally. Verify with a lockfile (bun.lockb) and consider a vendored copy or a published npm release.

findings.title: Subprocess spawn passes full process.env to children, including secrets
findings.description: all.ts spawns each Cat runner via spawn('bun', [script], { env: process.env }), forwarding ANTHROPIC_API_KEY/OPENAI_API_KEY/GROQ_API_KEY and any other env vars unconditionally. Combined with the unpinned gbrain dependency and adversarial PDF parsing, this widens the blast radius if a Cat runner ingests an untrusted artifact. CWE-200: Exposure of Sensitive Information. Acceptable for a dev tool, but worth limiting.
findings.recommendation: Pass an explicit env subset to children — only the keys that Cat actually needs. Cats that don't call LLMs (e.g., Cat 10 adversarial structural tests) shouldn't see API keys.

findings.title: Multiple uses of `any` type and eslint-disable bypasses in agent adapter
findings.description: claude-sonnet-with-tools.ts contains 3+ `// eslint-disable-next-line @typescript-eslint/no-explicit-any` comments and uses `any` for messages content and engine cast. This weakens compile-time guarantees on the agent loop's most error-prone code path (tool_use/tool_result message construction).
findings.recommendation: Replace `any` with proper Anthropic SDK types: use `Anthropic.Messages.MessageParam` for messages and `Anthropic.Messages.ContentBlock`/`ToolResultBlockParam` for content arrays. Add an `AgentEngine` interface with a `disconnect?()` method instead of casting engine to `any`.

findings.title: Bug in writeDocs path construction — dead/confusing code
findings.description: In amara-life-gen.ts writeDocs(), the line `const path = join(CORPUS_ROOT, slugPath + '.md'.replace(/\.md$/, '') === slugPath ? slugPath : slugPath);` is computed but never used (fullPath is built independently and used). The expression is also semantically nonsensical: `'.md'.replace(/\.md$/, '')` always equals `''`, so `slugPath + '' === slugPath` is always true, making the ternary dead. This is confusing dead code that suggests a prior bug attempt.
findings.recommendation: Remove the unused `const path = ...` line entirely. Keep only `const fullPath = join(CORPUS_ROOT, slugPath);` and the writeFileSync call. Add a unit test that writeDocs writes to the expected paths.

findings.title: Silent console suppression in HybridNoGraphAdapter.init swallows real errors
findings.description: HybridNoGraphAdapter.init monkey-patches `console.log` and `console.error` to no-ops during importFromContent. If importFromContent emits a real error (rate-limit, schema mismatch), it's invisible. The try/finally restores them, but during the import window any error message is lost — making bench failures hard to diagnose.
findings.recommendation: Capture suppressed messages into a buffer and either log them on error or expose a debug flag. At minimum, only suppress console.log and let console.error pass through; errors should always surface.

findings.title: all.ts uses CommonJS require() inside ES module
findings.description: readCommit() and readBranch() use `const { execSync } = require('child_process');` inside an ES module file (package.json declares `"type": "module"`). While Bun tolerates this, it's inconsistent with the file's `import` statements at the top and breaks under stricter loaders. Also, both functions are wrapped in `new Promise` despite being purely synchronous.
findings.recommendation: Move `import { execSync } from 'child_process';` to the top alongside `import { spawn } ...`. Make readCommit/readBranch synchronous functions returning string. Remove unnecessary Promise wrappers.

findings.title: Incorrect grouping plural in renderRail (companys/persons)
findings.description: renderWorldHtml generates type plurals as `${type}s`, producing 'companys' and 'persons'. The world-html.test.ts test asserts these exact strings, so the test enforces the bug. While intentional per the comment, it's user-facing in the explorer UI.
findings.recommendation: Use a small lookup map: `{person: 'people', company: 'companies', meeting: 'meetings', concept: 'concepts'}`. Update the test accordingly. Cheap fix, improves the contributor-facing world.html.

findings.title: Code duplication in injection helpers (createRng, pick, escapeRegex)
findings.description: adversarial-injections.ts duplicates `createRng` (Mulberry32) and `pick<T>` from amara-life.ts verbatim, with a comment acknowledging it ('matches amara-life.ts'). Six injectXxx functions also share boilerplate: pick rng, pick realTarget, build content, return goldDelta. Reduces maintainability — a fix to one PRNG must be ported.
findings.recommendation: Extract `createRng`, `pick`, and `escapeRegex` to a shared `eval/util/random.ts` module. Add a per-injection helper `buildResult(content, mustExtract, mustNotExtract, note)` to flatten the six similar return shapes.

findings.title: Test for renderRail relies on pluralization bug rather than feature
findings.description: world-html.test.ts asserts `expect(html).toContain('companys');` — a comment in the source acknowledges 'imperfect plural but cheap'. Test is locked to the bug, so fixing pluralization requires editing the test. Indicates test-as-spec drift.
findings.recommendation: When fixing the pluralization (separate finding), update the test to assert the corrected forms ('companies', 'people', 'meetings', 'concepts'). Avoid pinning tests to known bugs.

findings.title: Cat 5/8/9 'programmatic-only' runners lack external harness documentation
findings.description: eval/runner/all.ts explicitly skips Cat 5 (provenance), Cat 8 (skill compliance), and Cat 9 (workflows) because they require runtime inputs (claims, probes, scenarios, pre-seeded state). The code says 'Run via runCatN({...}) from a harness' but no harness, example, or test fixture is referenced. A contributor reading the report cannot reproduce these three categories — yet they're part of the 12-category BrainBench scorecard and likely the most differentiating ones (Cat 8 brain-first compliance, Cat 9 end-to-end). This is a critical reproducibility gap for a public benchmark.
findings.recommendation: Add an example harness file (e.g., eval/runner/harness/programmatic-cats.ts) demonstrating how to invoke runCat5/runCat8/runCat9 with sample inputs, and document this in eval/RUNBOOK.md. At minimum, the report's 'Programmatic-only Cats' section should link to a working example and gold-file location.

findings.title: Generator scripts assume undocumented .env.testing file with cross-worktree discovery
findings.description: Both eval/generators/gen.ts and eval/generators/amara-life-gen.ts require a .env.testing file at the repo root and throw with a cryptic message instructing users to 'Copy it from a sibling worktree'. There is no documented onboarding path for a fresh contributor who has no sibling worktree. The .env.testing format (which keys, how quoting works) is parsed by an inline regex but never specified in user-facing docs. For a public benchmark advertised as reproducible, this is a major friction point.
findings.recommendation: Provide an .env.testing.example template at the repo root listing required keys (ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, OPENAI_API_KEY, GROQ_API_KEY) with placeholder values and a comment block. Document in eval/RUNBOOK.md how to obtain each key and which Cats need which key. Update the error message to point to the example file rather than a sibling-worktree hack.

findings.title: Adapter contract (Adapter interface) is referenced everywhere but never documented in one place
findings.description: Five adapter implementations (grep-only, vector, vector-grep-rrf-fusion, claude-sonnet-with-tools, gbrain) all implement an `Adapter` interface from '../types.ts' with init/query/teardown/snapshot methods and AdapterConfig/BrainState/RankedDoc types — but no single doc explains the contract for contributors who want to add an EXT-4 adapter. The agent adapter even throws on query() with a long inline comment justifying the design, which is exactly the kind of contract-level decision that belongs in CONTRIBUTING.md, not in a thrown error.
findings.recommendation: Add an 'Adding an adapter' section to eval/CONTRIBUTING.md covering: (1) the Adapter interface methods and their semantics, (2) what RankedDoc/BrainState/AdapterConfig require, (3) when to throw on query() vs returning [], (4) snapshot semantics, (5) which scorecards (retrieval vs Cat 8/9) the adapter opts into, (6) a link to grep-only.ts as the canonical reference implementation.

findings.title: Adding a new Tier 5.5 query / category lacks end-to-end contributor walkthrough
findings.description: eval/cli/query-new.ts and query-validate.ts produce/check Tier 5.5 query JSON, and queries/index.ts mentions a path 'eval/external-authors/<author-slug>/queries.json'. But nothing visible documents the full Tier 5.5 PR flow: where the file goes, how it gets included in the runner, naming conventions for author slugs, what tags are valid, how `as_of_date` interacts with temporal verbs at scoring time, what 'expected_abstention' means for an adapter, or how a contributor previews their query against a corpus. The CLI help text says 'submit a PR' but the PR template / review criteria aren't referenced.
findings.recommendation: Add an 'Authoring a Tier 5.5 query' section to eval/CONTRIBUTING.md that walks through: scaffold → fill gold.relevant → run validator → run a single-query smoke (e.g., new `eval:query:try` script) → submit PR. Include a worked example with a non-trivial query, gold rationale, and the expected scorecard line. Document the eval/external-authors/ directory layout and PR review criteria.

findings.title: Adversarial injection kinds defined in code but no doc maps them to Cat 6 / Cat 10 scoring semantics
findings.description: eval/runner/adversarial-injections.ts defines 6 InjectionKind values (code_fence_leak, inline_code_slug, substring_collision, ambiguous_role, prose_only_mention, multi_entity_sentence) and emits GoldDelta with must_extract/must_not_extract arrays. The code comments say results flow into 'eval/data/world-v1-adversarial/_adversarial/{slug}.json' for the Cat 6 scorer to compute per-kind precision/recall/FPR — but a contributor adding a new kind has no spec for: (a) the JSON schema of the metadata file, (b) how the scorer aggregates per-kind metrics, (c) what 'mentions' vs typed link types semantically mean across the codebase. Adding a 7th kind requires reading scorer source.
findings.recommendation: Add an 'Adding an adversarial injection kind' subsection to eval/CONTRIBUTING.md documenting: (1) the InjectionKind enum, (2) GoldDelta semantics (must_extract type values, when must_not_extract is required), (3) how Cat 6 aggregates per-kind metrics, (4) how to add a fixture and have it picked up by cat6-prose-scale.ts, (5) examples of good vs over-fitted injections.

findings.title: Cost / budget guidance scattered across files without a central RUNBOOK section
findings.description: Cost-relevant constants are sprinkled: gen.ts has HARD_STOP_USD=80, amara-life-gen.ts has HARD_STOP_USD=20, claude-sonnet-with-tools.ts has hardcoded Sonnet 4.6 prices, package.json has eval:brainbench:published with 'N=10', and all.ts mentions '~$200 Opus' for the published run. A new contributor running `bun run eval:brainbench:published` cannot easily see the projected total cost, which models are billed, or where the daily caps come from. This is a real footgun for an MIT-licensed public benchmark where anyone might run it.
findings.recommendation: Add a 'Cost & rate limits' section to eval/RUNBOOK.md tabulating: smoke ($0), iteration N=5 (~$X), published N=10 (~$200), per-Cat cost breakdown, which Cats use which models (Opus/Sonnet/Haiku/embedding), where hard-stop caps are set, and how to override them. Cross-reference the constants in gen.ts and amara-life-gen.ts.

findings.title: Slug regex referenced by line number is fragile cross-file documentation
findings.description: amara-life.ts line 28 says 'Slug convention (matches eval/runner/queries/validator.ts:131 regex)'. Pinning a line number in a sibling file is a documentation anti-pattern — any edit to validator.ts shifts the reference and silently rots. The slug regex is clearly load-bearing (it's checked in validator, generated in skeleton, referenced in injection kinds) but isn't documented in a stable canonical location.
findings.recommendation: Define the canonical slug regex as a single named exported constant (e.g., `SLUG_REGEX` in eval/runner/queries/validator.ts) and document its grammar (allowed chars, dir/slug shape, max length) in a 'Slug spec' section of eval/CONTRIBUTING.md. Replace line-number references with imports of the constant or links to the doc section.

findings.title: world-html.ts XSS-safety design comment is excellent but not surfaced to contributors
findings.description: eval/generators/world-html.ts has a thorough module-level comment explaining XSS escaping rationale, the markdown-not-rendered tradeoff, and a 'High-confidence vuln class, 9/10' callout. world-html.test.ts has matching tests including a real XSS attack vector. This is genuinely good inline documentation. However, this design rule ('Opus-generated content must always pass through escapeHtml before insertion') is a project-wide invariant that future contributors building other renderers (e.g., a benchmark report HTML renderer) will need. It should be promoted from this one file's header to a SECURITY.md or to CONTRIBUTING.md's renderer guidance.
findings.recommendation: Promote the XSS-escaping rule to a 'Rendering LLM-generated content' subsection in eval/CONTRIBUTING.md (or a brief SECURITY.md), referencing escapeHtml in world-html.ts as the canonical helper. Acknowledge the existing tests as the contract.

findings.title: package.json scripts have no inline description; eval:* commands rely on RUNBOOK
findings.description: package.json defines 14 eval:* scripts (eval:run, eval:run:dev, eval:world:view, eval:query:validate, eval:query:new, eval:type-accuracy, eval:generate-amara-life, eval:generate-amara-life:dry, eval:brainbench, eval:brainbench:smoke, eval:brainbench:published, eval:cat6, eval:cat11). Several have BRAINBENCH_N / BRAINBENCH_CONCURRENCY env-var overrides baked in, but there's no `npm-scripts:help` style listing or doc table mapping each script to: what it does, expected runtime, expected cost, prerequisite data files. CLI scripts have inline --help (good), but the package.json scripts as a surface don't.
findings.recommendation: In eval/RUNBOOK.md, add a table listing every eval:* script with columns: command, purpose, runtime, cost ($ estimate), prereqs (env vars, generated corpora). Alternatively, add a `bun run eval:help` script that prints this table.

findings.title: Missing lockfile in repository
findings.description: The provided file listing shows package.json but no bun.lockb, package-lock.json, or yarn.lock. Without a committed lockfile, dependency resolution is non-deterministic across developers, CI, and time — which directly undermines the BrainBench benchmark's reproducibility claims (the report includes commit hashes and presents itself as a 'published baseline'). Caret ranges on @anthropic-ai/sdk (^0.30.0) and pdf-parse (^2.4.5) compound this risk.
findings.recommendation: Run `bun install` and commit the resulting `bun.lockb` to the repo. Update .gitignore to ensure the lockfile is NOT ignored. Add a CI check that fails if the lockfile is out of sync (`bun install --frozen-lockfile`).

findings.title: Git dependency pinned to mutable branch (master) instead of commit SHA
findings.description: `gbrain` is sourced from `github:garrytan/gbrain#master` — pinning to a branch ref. Any push to master in the upstream repo silently changes what users install with no version bump, breaking reproducibility of every benchmark run and creating a supply-chain risk (a compromised or rewritten master would propagate to everyone running `bun install`). This is especially severe for a 'published benchmark' that consumers cite numerically.
findings.recommendation: Pin gbrain to an immutable commit SHA: `"gbrain": "github:garrytan/gbrain#<40-char-sha>"`. Better, publish gbrain to npm (or a private registry) with semver and consume `"gbrain": "^X.Y.Z"`. Pair with the lockfile fix.

findings.title: @types/bun pinned to 'latest' — non-reproducible dev environment
findings.description: `"@types/bun": "latest"` resolves to whatever the npm registry serves at install time. Combined with the missing lockfile, two developers running `bun install` on the same commit can get different TypeScript types, leading to inconsistent type-checking results. 'latest' is widely considered an anti-pattern.
findings.recommendation: Replace with a concrete semver range, e.g. `"@types/bun": "^1.1.0"` (or whatever matches the Bun runtime version targeted). Commit a lockfile so the resolved version is reproducible.

findings.title: pdf-parse declared as devDependency but unused in shown sources / mis-classified
findings.description: `pdf-parse` is listed under devDependencies. Cat 11 (multi-modal ingestion) likely uses it at eval time, which is dev-context here, so the placement is defensible — but pdf-parse historically has had a known issue where importing the package executes a debug code path that reads `./test/data/*.pdf` from the install location (causing crashes with 'ENOENT: ./test/data/05-versions-space.pdf'). This is a known footgun in pdf-parse 1.x; v2.x (which 2.4.5 is) reportedly fixed it but the package is sparsely maintained. Verify the current import path doesn't trigger the debug code, and consider alternatives like `pdfjs-dist` or `unpdf` which are more actively maintained.
findings.recommendation: Verify pdf-parse 2.4.5 doesn't trigger debug-mode side effects on import. If it does, switch to `unpdf` or `pdfjs-dist`. If the dependency is only used at eval time and not by downstream consumers of this package, keeping it in devDependencies is correct.

findings.title: Runtime dependency on Bun without engines field declaration
findings.description: Every script in package.json invokes `bun` directly (e.g., `bun test`, `bun eval/runner/multi-adapter.ts`). The package uses Bun-specific features (`import.meta.main`, top-level await, `.ts` direct execution, `bun:test`). However, package.json has no `engines` field declaring the required Bun version, and no `packageManager` field. A contributor with the wrong Bun version will hit confusing errors. The README/CONTRIBUTING is the only signal of the required runtime.
findings.recommendation: Add `"engines": { "bun": ">=1.1.0" }` (or the actual minimum tested Bun version) and `"packageManager": "bun@1.1.x"` to package.json. Document this in CONTRIBUTING.md as well.

findings.title: No automated dependency update tooling configured
findings.description: The provided file listing does not include `.github/dependabot.yml`, `renovate.json`, or `.github/workflows/*` showing automated dependency updates. Given the project pins to a 0.x SDK and a mutable git ref, drift is likely without automation. For a benchmark expected to remain reproducible across published baselines (N=10, $200 Opus), drift detection is critical to know when re-baselining is needed.
findings.recommendation: Add a Dependabot config (.github/dependabot.yml) with weekly updates for npm + github-actions ecosystems. Alternatively configure Renovate. Pair this with the lockfile fix so PRs are meaningful.

findings.title: Implicit dependency on subpath imports from gbrain (deep imports)
findings.description: Multiple adapters import from gbrain subpaths: `gbrain/pglite-engine`, `gbrain/search/hybrid`, `gbrain/import-file`, `gbrain/embedding`, `gbrain/link-extraction`, `gbrain/types`. Deep subpath imports are fragile because they bypass the package's public API surface — any internal refactor in gbrain (which is pinned to a mutable master branch) silently breaks BrainBench. Combined with the master-branch pin, this means any internal reorg in gbrain breaks `bun install` users with no semver signal.
findings.recommendation: (1) Pin gbrain to an immutable SHA. (2) Push gbrain maintainers to declare these subpaths in `exports` field of gbrain's package.json so they become part of the supported public API. (3) Add a build-time smoke test that verifies all `from 'gbrain/*'` imports resolve.

findings.title: License declared MIT but no LICENSE file referenced; gbrain transitive license unverified
findings.description: package.json declares `"license": "MIT"`, which is fine, but the gbrain dependency (sourced from a GitHub repo, not npm) does not have its license verified in the supply chain — it could be MIT, AGPL, or unlicensed. For a benchmark labeled MIT and consumed as a library, downstream users assume transitive license compatibility. The corpus manifest also writes `license: 'MIT'` (eval/generators/amara-life-gen.ts line ~310).
findings.recommendation: Verify gbrain's LICENSE file in its repository and confirm it's MIT-compatible. Add a LICENSE file to this repo if not already present. Consider running `license-checker` in CI to enumerate transitive license types once gbrain is pinned to a SHA.

findings.title: Sequential per-item LLM generation in amara-life-gen wastes wall time
findings.description: All four item types (50 emails, 300 slack messages, 8 meetings, 40 notes — ~398 LLM calls total) are generated in serial `for...of await` loops. With Opus latency typically 5-15s per call, this means ~30-100 minutes of wall time even though Anthropic supports concurrent requests. The HARD_STOP_USD check is the only coordinated state, which would parallelize cleanly with a small p-limit pool (e.g., 4-8). Cost is unchanged; only wall time improves dramatically (~4-8x speedup).
findings.recommendation: Wrap each batch (emails, slack, meetings, notes) with a bounded concurrency pool (e.g., `p-limit(6)` or hand-rolled worker queue like the one in `gen.ts`). Read concurrency from env (`BRAINBENCH_LLM_CONCURRENCY`) for parity with all.ts. Guard the HARD_STOP_USD check with the running tracker.usd before queueing the next call.

findings.title: all.ts ignores BRAINBENCH_LLM_CONCURRENCY across child subprocesses
findings.description: The dispatcher runs up to 2 subprocess Cats concurrently (BRAINBENCH_CONCURRENCY), and each child independently consumes BRAINBENCH_LLM_CONCURRENCY. With concurrency=2 and LLM_CONCURRENCY=4, the actual peak Anthropic concurrency is 8, not 4. There is no global coordinator. This silently exceeds rate limits and budget caps that operators believe they configured.
findings.recommendation: Either (a) document that effective LLM concurrency = subprocess_concurrency × LLM_CONCURRENCY, or (b) divide BRAINBENCH_LLM_CONCURRENCY by the subprocess concurrency before exporting it to children, or (c) use a token-bucket file lock / IPC server so children share a single LLM budget. (b) is the simplest correct fix.

findings.title: VectorOnlyAdapter scores cosine over every doc on every query (O(N×D) full scan)
findings.description: query() iterates `s.vectors` (size N) and computes cosine against every page vector — a full O(N×D) scan on each call. For the 240-page corpus this is ~240×3072 = 737K float ops per query (fast), but if the corpus or query set grows (e.g., Cat 6 prose-scale runs 500+ pages with N=10 reruns = 5000+ queries), latency scales linearly. Also, the cosine loop is per-element JS — no SIMD, no normalized-vector dot-product fast path.
findings.recommendation: Pre-normalize stored vectors to unit length at init time so query reduces to a dot product (drop two of the three sqrt/div ops). For larger corpora consider an HNSW or flat-IVF index (e.g., hnswlib-node) with a top-K cutoff. Even without an ANN index, batching the dot products into a single Float32Array matrix multiplication via a typed-array loop yields ~2x speedup.

findings.title: HybridNoGraphAdapter init silences console globally — leaks across concurrent code
findings.description: init() reassigns `console.log` and `console.error` to no-ops globally during importFromContent. If any concurrent task (e.g., another adapter init under multi-adapter.ts, a background timer, or a logging callback in p-limit) runs during this window, its output is silently dropped. With BRAINBENCH_CONCURRENCY=2 and multiple adapters initializing concurrently, this race is realistic. The try/finally restores them, but the global is shared across all isolates in the same process.
findings.recommendation: Pass a logger option into importFromContent (preferred), or capture/restore using a dedicated console proxy that only suppresses calls from the current async context (AsyncLocalStorage). At minimum, document that init() must run serially. Also: restoring in `finally` doesn't help if init throws and another adapter is mid-init in parallel.

findings.title: claude-sonnet-with-tools rate-limit backoff doesn't honor Retry-After header
findings.description: On 429/529 errors the loop sleeps `1000 * 2^attempt` ms (1s, 2s, 4s) regardless of the Retry-After header Anthropic returns. With max 3 retries and a 30-60s server-suggested wait, all retries can fire well before the bucket refills, exhausting the retry budget and bubbling the error. This wastes the partial agent-loop work already paid for (every prior turn's tokens).
findings.recommendation: Read `err.headers?.['retry-after']` (or the SDK's parsed equivalent) when the error is a rate-limit; honor that value capped at e.g. 60s; fall back to exponential backoff only when no header is present. Also consider raising maxRetries default to 5 and adding jitter (±20%) to avoid thundering herd when many agents hit the limit together.

findings.title: Agent loop appends full message history every turn — token cost grows quadratically
findings.description: Each turn appends the full assistant response (including tool_use blocks) and tool_result blocks back into `messages`, then re-sends the entire history on the next call. Tool results can be large (search returning 10+ chunks of compiled_truth), so input tokens grow O(turns²). With turnCap=10 and large tool outputs, the last turn can send 30K+ input tokens repeatedly. The `cache_control: ephemeral` is only set on the system prompt — not on the growing message history, where it would matter most.
findings.recommendation: Apply `cache_control: { type: 'ephemeral' }` to the last static prefix of `messages` each turn (Anthropic's prompt-cache supports up to 4 cache breakpoints; one on system + one on the last assistant turn captures most savings). Additionally, truncate tool_result content blocks to a budget (e.g., 4KB) — `bridge.executeTool` already returns `truncated: boolean`, suggesting truncation logic exists; ensure it's used aggressively. Could cut input tokens by 50-80%.

findings.title: Subprocess output buffered unboundedly in memory in all.ts
findings.description: Each child's stdout+stderr is concatenated into `output` string with no cap. A long-running Cat (e.g., Cat 6 prose-scale at N=10, or Cat 11 multimodal) emitting verbose logs over 10 minutes can produce 100+ MB of output, multiplied by concurrency=2 in-flight = 200+ MB of strings held by the parent. The full output is then written into a single markdown file, which itself can become unwieldy.
findings.recommendation: Cap `output` at e.g. 1 MB per child — keep first 100KB and last 900KB with a `[... truncated N bytes ...]` marker between (most useful: setup + final summary). Alternatively, stream child output to a per-Cat log file and only embed the tail in the markdown report.

findings.title: VectorOnlyAdapter init batches embeddings serially despite batch loop
findings.description: The init loop calls `await embedBatch(batch)` for each batch of 50 in series. embedBatch presumably issues one OpenAI request per batch, so batches are serialized — for 240 pages that's 5 sequential OpenAI calls, each ~1-3s. Could run them concurrently (e.g., 2-3 in flight) given OpenAI's per-org rate limits accommodate this. Even on the 240-page corpus this saves ~5-10s; on Cat 6's 500+ pages it's ~30s.
findings.recommendation: Use a small concurrency pool (e.g., 3 parallel embedBatch calls) when issuing batches. embedBatch should already handle retries internally; concurrent issuance is safe within OpenAI rate limits at this corpus size.

findings.title: BM25 candidate union scored individually instead of accumulated in a single pass
findings.description: RipgrepBm25Adapter.query first builds a candidate Set by unioning postings for all query tokens, then iterates the Set and re-scores each doc — re-walking the postings for every query token per doc. A single pass over query-token postings, accumulating partial scores per doc into a Map, would be ~2x faster (avoid re-traversing postings indexed by query). Negligible on the 240-page corpus, but Cat 6 scales to 500+ pages × 100+ queries.
findings.recommendation: Accumulate scores in one pass: for each query token, look up its posting once, iterate (docId, tf) entries, add `idf * tf * (k1+1) / (tf + k1*(1-b+b*docLen/avgDocLength))` to a running scoreMap[docId]. Skip the candidate Set entirely. Eliminates redundant posting lookups.

findings.title: Adversarial test runs 30s timeout per op via Promise.race — leaks setTimeout handles
findings.description: tryOp() races the operation against a setTimeout(30s, reject). When the operation completes first (the common case), the setTimeout is never cleared — the timer remains scheduled until 30s elapses. With ~7 ops per case × 25 cases = 175 timers, all alive for up to 30s, this is harmless but inelegant and prevents fast process exit (Bun keeps the loop alive while timers exist).
findings.recommendation: Capture the timer handle and clearTimeout it on race completion. Or use AbortController + AbortSignal.timeout(30000) in newer Bun.

cross_cutting_insights: arch-009, qual-003, and sec-010 are the same defect (dead `path` line in writeDocs) reported across three dimensions — fix once, resolve all three.

sec-007, dep-001, and dep-008 form a chain: gbrain pinned to mutable master + deep subpath imports + no lockfile = compound supply-chain/reproducibility risk for a 'published baseline' benchmark. Pinning to a SHA + committing bun.lockb addresses all three.
arch-007, qual-011, and arch-006 reflect a missing eval/lib/ shared utilities layer (PRNG, pick, escapeRegex, seed data). A single refactor to extract eval/lib/{rng,seed-data}.ts addresses all three.

arch-008, doc-006, and perf-001 all stem from the absent shared LLM-budget/cost module — extracting eval/lib/llm-budget.ts unifies cost tracking, enables global concurrency coordination, and provides a single doc surface.
arch-011, qual-007, and perf-003 are the same console-monkey-patching defect viewed from architecture, quality, and performance lenses; one fix (logger parameter to importFromContent) resolves all.
doc-001 (missing harness for Cats 5/8/9) and arch-004 (ad-hoc subprocess vs programmatic dispatch) are the same architectural gap — a unified CatRunner interface with a documented harness fixes both.

perf-006 (quadratic token growth) and sec-004 (errors echoed into tool_result) both touch the agent loop's message-construction path; auditing the loop should address both, plus enable proper SDK typing per qual-002.

doc-007 (line-number reference to slug regex) and arch-005 (deep relative imports) reflect the missing barrel/contracts module — an eval/contracts/index.ts exporting SLUG_REGEX and shared types fixes both.
